newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Higher Indonesian cocoa crop seen as season ends.
newsitem.headline: Higher Indonesian cocoa crop seen as season ends.

text.p: Indonesia's cocoa output in the 1995/1996 (October/September) season, now approaching its end, is expected to be higher than the previous period, traders said on Wednesday, though forecasts differed by 40,000 tonnes.
"We estimate Indonesia's cocoa output in October/September 1996 will reach 270,000 tonnes against 250,000 in the same period of 1994/95," one Jakarta-based cocoa trader said.

One trader based in Ujung Pandang, south Sulawesi said cocoa output was expected to reach 260,000 tonnes this year with the main cocoa producing island of Sulawesi expected to supply between 140,000 to 150,000 tonnes of the total output.
Regional traders, however, said Indonesia's cocoa output in 1995/96 season could be as high as 290,000 to 300,000 tonnes.

They said the crop looked in good shape despite some concern about floods on the key growing island of Sulawesi and earlier concerns over the pod borer pest, a larva that burrows into cocoa pods and harms the beans.
"Our estimate of the Indonesian crop is between 290,000 and 300,000 tonnes," a senior trader in a Western commodity house told Reuters in an interview. "Pod borer has not affected the crop at all."
Another leading dealer said the crop will probably reach 290,000 tonnes, although "it's going to be quite late" and will not be completely harvested until mid-October.

"There was some early reports of pod borer, but we understand it was dealt with quite efficiently by cutting down the infected trees. There is also some concern about floods on Sulawesi, but a lot of the crop looks quite good," he said.

Indonesian traders nevertheless agreed that domestic cocoa prices were likely to trend stable to lower, despite steady local demand, due to expected higher supply following the start of the mid-crop (minor harvest) in Sulawesi.
They said cocoa was currently trading at 2,775-2,800 rupiah/kg compared with 2,800-2,825 rupiah in late August.
"Output from the mid-crop has started entering the market and supply is likely to be affected soon," another dealer in the south Sulawesi's city of Ujung Pandang said.
"Prices, however, are likely to be stable to trend slightly lower as cocoa demand in the domestic market is seen firm," he said.
"Around 96,000 tonnes of Sulawesi's output is expected to go for exports, while the rest will meet the sustained strong local demand especially for companies on Java island," he added.

This year's cocoa harvest will make Indonesia the third largest producer in the world behind the Ivory Coast and Ghana. The Ivorian crop could reach 950,000 tonnes this season while Ghanian output may touch 400,000 tonnes.

Traders believe the expansion of plantings on Indonesia will propel the country to become the second biggest producer of cocoa by the turn of the century. Cocoa is the main ingredient in the production of chocolates.
